summary:
Bengkulu is a province of Indonesia, and trans visitors here stand under Indonesia's national legal and policy framework. No Bengkulu-specific statute, enforcement action, protection measure, service or documented incident directed at trans people appears in the sources; the province is assessed on national conditions.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is not itself criminalised in private in Indonesia outside the provinces with their own provisions. There are, however, no anti-discrimination protections for lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people anywhere in the country.

The amended national penal code, signed in December 2022, took effect on 2 January 2026. Its provision on consensual sex outside marriage is the principal route by which same-sex activity becomes prosecutable, because Indonesia does not permit same-sex marriage and so no same-sex relationship qualifies as marital. Reporting indicates prosecutions under this provision are selective rather than systematic, and the offence is actionable on complaint by an immediate family member, carrying up to one year's imprisonment under the Wikipedia account of the amendment (the parent framework text cites up to two years).

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity directly, alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025. Bengkulu has no such provincial provision documented.

Physical risk to trans people is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs attacked trans women across Indonesia in a wave from 14 to 16 July 2026, including more than 15 trans women doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage shared online. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists 'the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture' among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy. A researcher cited in the same reporting documents markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016.

Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy. On 11 August 2025 three men were arrested over a Facebook community page.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; in March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option. Legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025. A 2025 Pew survey found 93% of Indonesians rated homosexuality morally unacceptable.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources give two different maximum penalties for the penal code's sex-outside-marriage provision: the parent framework text states up to two years' imprisonment, while the Wikipedia account cited in the inventory states up to one year. Both figures are carried here as reported; the discrepancy is unresolved.

No usable finding was documented for Bengkulu from its own Wikipedia entry, so the province-level assessment rests entirely on national material. Whether Bengkulu provincial authorities have issued any moral or public-order ordinance, or conducted any raid or arrest on LGBT-related grounds, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The inventory does not document Bengkulu-specific healthcare access, shelter provision, or police handling of complaints by trans residents; these are not sourced rather than confirmed absent.
